transcript:
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Rylan Barton.
After an emergency hearing today, a federal judge is expected to decide soon whether to
restore access to journalists, whom President Trump recently banned from the White House.
Lawyers representing CNN, Politico and MS Now argued it was a matter of constitutional
rights, NPR's Julianna Kim reports.
An attorney representing the news outlets argued that the abrupt ban violated reporters
First Amendment and Fifth Amendment rights, which relate to free speech and due process.
The lawyer also called it retaliation for the news outlets' critical coverage of the
president.
In response, a lawyer at the Justice Department argued that access to the White House is
a privilege, not a right.
The federal judge who listened to these arguments did not make a ruling on the bench.
He said he'll consider both sides and give an answer as soon as possible.
Julianna Kim, NPR News.
Israel's war against Hamas in Gaza has been a major topic during the UN General Assembly
in New York, as several world leaders have used their speeches to bluntly criticize Israel's
conduct.
That's as Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is set to speak tomorrow, as NPR's Kat Lonsdorf
reports.
UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres first condemned the Hamas-led attack on Israel in
2023, but then said what followed by Israel was a "onslot" on Palestinians in Gaza.
He also said Israeli violence and settlement expansion in the Israeli-occupied West Bank
is raising the "spector of ethnic cleansing."
Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan described Gaza as a "concentration camp," while Jordan's
King Abdullah II said Israel is a "regional threat" that operates with "terrifying levels
of impunity."
Netanyahu has yet to directly respond to much of the criticism, but is set to land in New
York on Thursday, address the UN, and return to Israel, all in the same day.
Kat Lonsdorf, NPR News, Tel Aviv.
A Costa Rican migrant has died in ICE custody, making him the 58th detainee to die at a detention
facility since President Trump returned to office, and PR's Vanessa Romo reports.
Carlos Jose Marchena died on September 18, according to ICE officials, who told NPR that
Marchena was found unresponsive by staff at the Wynn Correctional Center.
He was eventually transferred to a nearby hospital, but despite life-saving efforts,
the 36-year-old could not be revived.
The official cause of death remains pending further medical examination.
But Marchena's sister told Costa Rican news outlets that her brother said he was denied
adequate medical care and sufficient food and water to help control his diabetes.
She says he complained of chest pains just hours before he died.
ICE says Marchena received proper medical care.
An immigration judge ordered him removed from the U.S. in July following two criminal convictions
and an arrest for assault.
Vanessa Romo, NPR News.
Hurricane Polo is sent to skirt the Pacific coast of Mexico and could bring mudslides
and life-threatening flooding.
Forecasters say Polo is a major hurricane, with maximum sustained winds of 155 miles
an hour.
This is NPR.
Three people have filed lawsuits against Six Flags Magic Mountain in Valencia, California,
claiming they suffered traumatic brain injuries from the park's famous X-2 roller coaster.
The lawsuits follow a recent settlement over a wrongful death case involving the same ride
— the plaintiff's attorney says more than 100 clients have reported brain injuries from
the ride in the past two years, Six Flags since the ride has been closed since July 12.
More than five million people in Somalia are facing acute food insecurity, according to
the U.N., and weather projections show parts of the country may dip into famine in the
coming months.
NPR's Dury Buscarin reports.
Drowd and an insurgency by the militant group al-Shabaab have displaced millions of people
in Somalia.
Now, a super-el Nino in the Pacific Ocean could lead to serious floods.
Philip Lozinski of the Danish Refugee Council says they're working with the Somali government
to prepare evacuation sites.
"That's more or less what we can do, because I have to say that we are having much less
resources than we require for our planning.
And this is nowhere near to the needs that we see at the moment."
The U.S. suspended all aid to Somalia in January.
Other countries have also reduced assistance.
Dury Buscarin, NPR News.
The Oxford English Dictionary has officially added over a dozen Caribbean words.
Bimpert, a Bermudian term for a foolish person, is included.
Horner Mann from Trinidad and Tobago describes an unfaithful man.
The dictionary now holds around 500,000 words and phrases.
I'm Rylan Barton.
This is NPR News from Washington.

That's plus.npr.org.

topics.text: Federal judge considers whether to restore White House journalist access after Trump ban
Israeli conduct in Gaza criticized by world leaders at UN General Assembly
Costa Rican migrant Carlos Jose Marchena dies in ICE custody at Wynn Correctional Center
Hurricane Polo approaches Mexican Pacific coast with 155 mph winds, threatens flooding
Three people file lawsuits against Six Flags Magic Mountain over X-2 roller coaster injuries
More than five million Somalis facing acute food insecurity, potential famine conditions
Oxford English Dictionary adds over a dozen Caribbean words to its collection
